title: FAR U5·W1 — Cash, Receivables & Credit Losses (CECL)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the top of the balance sheet

The most liquid assets — cash and receivables — open every balance sheet, and they carry their own measurement rules. This week covers what counts as cash, the bank reconciliation that proves it, how accounts receivable are stated at net realizable value, and the modern current-expected-credit-loss (CECL) model that sets the allowance. For Meridian Building Group, where progress billings and retainage drive a large receivable balance, these accounts are where the audit and the financial statements begin.

Cash and cash equivalents

Cash includes coin, currency, and demand deposits available without restriction. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments with an original maturity of three months or less (Treasury bills, money-market funds). Items that are not cash include restricted cash (a compensating balance or a sinking fund — disclosed or classified separately), post-dated checks, and IOUs. The classification matters because cash and cash equivalents are the reconciling total on the statement of cash flows from FAR Unit 3.

The bank reconciliation

A bank reconciliation ties the book balance to the bank balance, isolating timing differences and errors. On the bank side, add deposits in transit and subtract outstanding checks; on the book side, add items the bank recorded that the company has not (interest earned, note collections) and subtract bank charges and NSF checks. Only the book-side adjustments generate journal entries, because they represent transactions the company has not yet recorded. The reconciliation is both a control and the support for the cash figure reported.

Accounts receivable at net realizable value

Trade receivables are recorded at the amount expected to be collected — net realizable value — which is the gross receivable minus the allowance for credit losses and any anticipated sales discounts and returns. Cash (sales) discounts (e.g., 2/10, net 30) may be recorded by the gross or net method. Because some customers will not pay, the receivable cannot be carried at its face amount — the allowance bridges the gap between what is owed and what will realistically be collected, keeping the asset faithfully stated.

The CECL model

Under ASC 326, the allowance is set by the current expected credit loss (CECL) model, which replaced the old incurred-loss method. CECL requires recognizing lifetime expected credit losses at origination — a day-one reserve — based on historical experience, current conditions, and reasonable and supportable forecasts. The result is generally a larger, earlier allowance than the incurred model, because the entity no longer waits for a loss to become probable. The allowance is a contra-asset; the period's change runs through credit loss expense.

Estimating and recording the allowance

Two estimation approaches are common. The percentage-of-sales method (income-statement approach) sets credit-loss expense as a percentage of credit sales, ignoring the existing allowance balance. The percentage-of-receivables / aging method (balance-sheet approach) computes the required ending allowance — often via an aging schedule applying higher loss rates to older buckets — and the entry is the amount needed to adjust the allowance to that target. Worked example: if aging indicates a required allowance of $90,000 and the account already has a $20,000 credit balance, the entry debits credit-loss expense and credits the allowance for $70,000. A specific write-off later debits the allowance and credits the receivable — with no effect on net receivables or expense.

Notes receivable

A note receivable is a written promise bearing interest. It is recorded at present value; if the stated rate differs from the market rate, the note is recorded at a discount or premium amortized to interest income using the effective-interest method from FAR Unit 2. A non-interest-bearing note is recorded net of an implied discount. Interest accrues over time (principal × rate × time), and a note received for goods or services is measured at the fair value of what was exchanged when the rate is unrealistic.

Financing receivables: factoring and pledging

A company can convert receivables to cash early. Pledging uses receivables as collateral for a loan (the receivables stay on the books, with disclosure). Factoring sells the receivables: without recourse, the buyer absorbs credit losses and the sale is final (derecognize the receivable, record a loss/fee); with recourse, the seller retains some risk, and whether it is a sale or a borrowing turns on whether control transferred. Assigning specific receivables is a financing midpoint. For MBG, factoring progress receivables can be a deliberate working-capital tool — at the cost of the factor's fee.

Internal control over cash

Because cash is the most liquid and most stolen asset, it carries the strongest internal controls: segregation of the custody, recording, and reconciliation functions; daily deposit of receipts intact; payment by pre-numbered check or electronic transfer with dual authorization; and an imprest petty-cash system replenished only with documented receipts. A lockbox arrangement, in which customers remit directly to a bank, removes cash from employees' hands entirely. These controls are the operational counterpart to the bank reconciliation — together they make the reported cash figure both accurate and safeguarded.

Presentation and disclosure of receivables

Receivables require disclosure beyond the single net number. The notes separate trade from nontrade receivables, disclose amounts pledged or factored, and present the allowance and the credit-quality information CECL demands — including a rollforward of the allowance and the aging of past-due balances. Receivables expected to be collected beyond one year are classified noncurrent. For MBG, retainage — amounts withheld by owners until a job is complete — is a receivable whose timing of collection must be disclosed, because it can sit on the books well past the normal cycle.

Discounting and dishonored notes

A holder needing cash early can discount a note receivable at a bank: the bank advances the maturity value (principal plus interest) less a discount computed on that maturity value for the remaining term. Whether the transfer is a sale or a borrowing again depends on recourse and control. If the maker later dishonors the note, the holder reclassifies it to an account receivable at maturity value (plus any protest fee) and assesses it for collectibility. These mechanics extend the same financing-versus-sale judgment that governs factored accounts to interest-bearing notes.

CMA bridge

The CMA program managed MBG's receivable turnover and cash conversion cycle; FAR governs how those same receivables are measured — net realizable value, the CECL allowance, and the accounting when they are factored for cash. The day-one CECL reserve directly affects the working-capital ratios the CFO reports.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify cash and cash equivalents (original maturity ≤ 3 months); exclude restricted cash, post-dated checks, IOUs.
  2. Prepare a bank reconciliation (bank side: + deposits in transit, − outstanding checks; book side: + collections, − NSF/charges → journal entries).
  3. State receivables at net realizable value; set the CECL allowance (lifetime expected losses, day one) via percentage-of-sales (expense) or aging (adjust to required balance).
  4. Record notes receivable at present value (effective-interest); account for pledging (collateral) vs factoring (sale, with/without recourse).

Recap: cash equivalents are highly liquid investments maturing in three months or less (restricted cash excluded); a bank reconciliation isolates timing differences, with only book-side items journalized; receivables are carried at net realizable value using the CECL allowance, which books lifetime expected losses at origination and is estimated by percentage-of-sales (expense) or aging (adjust the allowance to a required balance, e.g., a $70,000 entry to reach $90,000); notes receivable are measured at present value with effective-interest amortization; and receivables are monetized by pledging (collateral) or factoring (a sale, with or without recourse).

flashcards.back: Short-term, highly liquid investments with ORIGINAL maturity ≤ 3 months (T-bills, money-market funds). Restricted cash, post-dated checks, and IOUs are NOT cash.
Only BOOK-side adjustments (interest/notes collected, NSF, bank charges) get journal entries. Bank side: + deposits in transit, − outstanding checks (no entry).
Gross receivable − allowance for credit losses − anticipated sales discounts/returns.

Current expected credit loss model: recognize LIFETIME expected credit losses at origination (day-one reserve) using history, current conditions, and reasonable/supportable forecasts. Replaced incurred-loss.
% of sales (income-statement): expense = % × credit sales, ignore existing allowance. Aging (balance-sheet): compute required ending allowance, adjust the allowance up/down to that target.
Required allowance $90,000, existing credit balance $20,000 → entry: Dr credit-loss expense / Cr allowance $70,000.
Dr allowance, Cr accounts receivable. NO effect on net receivables or expense (both gross A/R and allowance drop).
Pledging: receivables are collateral for a loan (stay on books). Factoring: sell receivables — without recourse (buyer bears loss, final sale) or with recourse (seller retains risk).

questions.q: To qualify as a cash equivalent, an investment must have an original maturity of:
questions.explain: Cash equivalents are highly liquid investments with an original maturity of three months or less.

questions.q: In a bank reconciliation, which item requires a journal entry on the company's books?
choices: An NSF check returned by the bank
questions.explain: Only book-side items (NSF checks, bank charges, collections) are journalized; deposits in transit and outstanding checks adjust the bank side.

questions.q: The CECL model requires an entity to recognize:
choices: Lifetime expected credit losses at origination
Losses only when probable and incurred
questions.explain: ASC 326 (CECL) books lifetime expected credit losses on day one, replacing the incurred-loss model.

questions.q: Aging shows a required allowance of $90,000; the allowance has a $20,000 credit balance. The credit-loss entry is:
questions.explain: Under the balance-sheet (aging) approach, the entry adjusts the allowance to the target: $90,000 − $20,000 = $70,000.

questions.q: Writing off a specific uncollectible account:
choices: Has no effect on net realizable value
questions.explain: A write-off debits the allowance and credits A/R, leaving net receivables and expense unchanged.

choices: The buyer absorbs credit losses and the sale is final
The seller still bears all credit risk
The receivables stay on the seller's books as collateral
questions.explain: Without recourse, credit risk transfers to the factor and the receivables are derecognized.

questions.q: A non-interest-bearing note receivable is initially recorded at:
choices: Present value (net of the implied discount)
questions.explain: Notes receivable are recorded at present value; a non-interest-bearing note carries an implied discount amortized to interest income.
